title: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry
source_note: Standard advanced inorganic syllabus building on earlier coordination chemistry (CHM304) and inorganic chemistry (CHM303): crystal field/ligand field and MO bonding theories, organometallic chemistry and the 18-electron rule, catalysis by transition-metal complexes, bioinorganic chemistry, cluster and solid-state inorganic compounds, and f-block (lanthanide/actinide) chemistry.

questions.question: In crystal field theory, the splitting of d-orbitals in an octahedral complex produces:
options: A lower-energy t2g set (three orbitals) and a higher-energy eg set (two orbitals)
A lower-energy eg set and a higher-energy t2g set
Five degenerate orbitals with no splitting
A single non-degenerate orbital
questions.correct_answer: A lower-energy t2g set (three orbitals) and a higher-energy eg set (two orbitals)
questions.explanation: In an octahedral field, ligand point charges raise the energy of orbitals pointing directly at the ligands (dz2, dx2-y2, the eg set) relative to those pointing between ligands (dxy, dxz, dyz, the t2g set).

questions.question: In a tetrahedral complex, the crystal field splitting energy (Δt) compared with the octahedral splitting (Δo) for the same metal and ligands is:
options: Smaller, approximately 4/9 of Δo
Larger, approximately twice Δo
Exactly equal to Δo
Zero, tetrahedral complexes show no d-orbital splitting
questions.correct_answer: Smaller, approximately 4/9 of Δo
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral geometry has fewer ligands and none point directly at the orbital lobes, so the splitting is smaller; Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo, which is why tetrahedral complexes are almost always high-spin.

questions.question: The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by their ability to split d-orbitals. Which of the following is a strong-field ligand that typically produces low-spin complexes?
options: CN⁻
I⁻
Br⁻
F⁻
questions.correct_answer: CN⁻
questions.explanation: Cyanide is a strong π-acceptor ligand near the top of the spectrochemical series, producing a large Δo and favouring low-spin configurations.

questions.question: A complex is described as 'high spin' when:
options: Electrons occupy all d-orbitals singly (following Hund's rule) before pairing, because Δ is small relative to the pairing energy
All d-electrons are paired in the lowest-energy orbitals because Δ is large
The complex has no unpaired electrons
The metal is in a very high oxidation state
questions.correct_answer: Electrons occupy all d-orbitals singly (following Hund's rule) before pairing, because Δ is small relative to the pairing energy
questions.explanation: When the crystal field splitting Δ is smaller than the electron pairing energy (typically with weak-field ligands), electrons preferentially occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving a high-spin, more paramagnetic configuration.

questions.question: Ligand field theory improves upon simple crystal field theory mainly by:
options: Incorporating covalent metal-ligand orbital overlap through molecular orbital theory, rather than treating ligands as point charges
Ignoring the effect of ligands on d-orbital energies entirely
Applying only to organometallic compounds
Assuming purely ionic bonding with no orbital overlap
questions.correct_answer: Incorporating covalent metal-ligand orbital overlap through molecular orbital theory, rather than treating ligands as point charges
questions.explanation: Ligand field theory is essentially an MO-theory treatment of coordination complexes, accounting for covalency and π-bonding effects that purely electrostatic crystal field theory ignores.

questions.question: The Jahn-Teller effect predicts that a non-linear molecule with an electronically degenerate ground state will:
options: Distort geometrically to remove the degeneracy and lower its energy
Remain perfectly symmetric to preserve the degeneracy
Immediately dissociate
Only occur in tetrahedral complexes
questions.correct_answer: Distort geometrically to remove the degeneracy and lower its energy
questions.explanation: The Jahn-Teller theorem states that a non-linear degenerate electronic state is unstable and the molecule distorts (e.g. axial elongation in Cu(II) complexes) to remove the degeneracy and achieve a lower-energy configuration.

questions.question: The 18-electron rule in organometallic chemistry states that stable transition-metal complexes tend to have:
options: A total electron count (metal d-electrons plus electrons donated by ligands) of 18, filling all metal-based bonding/non-bonding valence orbitals
Exactly 18 ligands bound to the metal
18 valence electrons on each ligand
An oxidation state of +18
questions.correct_answer: A total electron count (metal d-electrons plus electrons donated by ligands) of 18, filling all metal-based bonding/non-bonding valence orbitals
questions.explanation: Analogous to the octet rule, many stable organometallic complexes achieve a noble-gas-like configuration with a total valence electron count of 18 (one 's', three 'p' and five 'd' metal-based orbitals filled).

questions.question: In ferrocene, Fe(C5H5)2, each cyclopentadienyl ring is best described as bonding to iron in what hapticity?
options: η5 (pentahapto)
η1 (monohapto)
η3 (trihapto)
η2 (dihapto)
questions.correct_answer: η5 (pentahapto)
questions.explanation: In ferrocene, each planar cyclopentadienyl ring bonds to the iron centre through all five carbon atoms simultaneously, described as η5-coordination, giving the characteristic sandwich structure.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide acts as a ligand in metal carbonyls primarily through:
options: σ-donation from carbon's lone pair to the metal, combined with π-backbonding from filled metal d-orbitals into the CO π* antibonding orbitals
Purely ionic bonding between C⁴⁻ and the metal cation
Hydrogen bonding between CO and the metal
π-donation only, with no σ-bonding component
questions.correct_answer: σ-donation from carbon's lone pair to the metal, combined with π-backbonding from filled metal d-orbitals into the CO π* antibonding orbitals
questions.explanation: The synergic bonding model for metal carbonyls involves CO donating its carbon lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO's π* orbitals, strengthening the M-C bond and weakening the C-O bond.

questions.question: Oxidative addition, a key step in many catalytic cycles of transition-metal complexes, involves:
options: A substrate adding to the metal centre with an increase in both the metal's oxidation state and its coordination number
A ligand leaving the metal centre, decreasing the coordination number
The metal being reduced while the coordination number decreases
Formation of a new metal-metal bond only
questions.correct_answer: A substrate adding to the metal centre with an increase in both the metal's oxidation state and its coordination number
questions.explanation: In oxidative addition, a molecule such as H2 or an alkyl halide adds across the metal, formally increasing the metal's oxidation state by two and its coordination number by two; the reverse process is reductive elimination.

questions.question: In homogeneous catalytic hydrogenation using Wilkinson's catalyst, RhCl(PPh3)3, the key mechanistic steps include:
options: Ligand dissociation, oxidative addition of H2, alkene coordination, migratory insertion, and reductive elimination
Simple physical adsorption of the alkene on a metal surface
Direct radical chain addition of H2 to the alkene with no metal involvement
Formation of a stable, isolable metal-alkane complex as the final catalytic product
questions.correct_answer: Ligand dissociation, oxidative addition of H2, alkene coordination, migratory insertion, and reductive elimination
questions.explanation: Wilkinson's catalyst operates via a well-established homogeneous catalytic cycle involving phosphine dissociation to open a site, oxidative addition of dihydrogen, alkene binding, migratory insertion of the alkene into the Rh-H bond, and reductive elimination of the alkane product.

questions.question: Metal clusters in inorganic chemistry are characterised by:
options: Direct metal-metal bonds linking three or more metal atoms within a single molecular unit
Metal atoms held together only by bridging halide ions with no direct metal-metal bonding
Isolated mononuclear metal complexes
Metal atoms dispersed in an inert solvent with no bonding interaction
questions.correct_answer: Direct metal-metal bonds linking three or more metal atoms within a single molecular unit
questions.explanation: Metal cluster compounds are defined by the presence of direct metal-metal bonding among three or more metal centres, often supported by bridging ligands, and are important in catalysis and materials chemistry.

questions.question: Bioinorganic chemistry studies the role of metal ions in biological systems. Which metal is central to the oxygen-carrying protein haemoglobin?
options: Iron (in a porphyrin/heme unit)
Zinc
Copper
Magnesium
questions.correct_answer: Iron (in a porphyrin/heme unit)
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin contains an Fe(II) ion coordinated within a heme (porphyrin) prosthetic group, which reversibly binds molecular oxygen for transport in blood.

questions.question: In chlorophyll, the central metal ion coordinated within the porphyrin-like ring is:
options: Magnesium
Iron
Cobalt
Manganese
questions.correct_answer: Magnesium
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is a magnesium-porphyrin (chlorin) complex; the Mg2+ ion sits at the centre of the tetrapyrrole ring and is essential for light absorption in photosynthesis.

questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is notable in bioinorganic chemistry for containing:
options: A cobalt ion coordinated within a corrin ring
A copper ion coordinated within a porphyrin ring
A zinc ion coordinated to four cysteine residues
A manganese cluster similar to photosystem II
questions.correct_answer: A cobalt ion coordinated within a corrin ring
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is unique among vitamins for containing a metal, cobalt, held within a corrin macrocycle (related to but distinct from a porphyrin), with the cobalt able to form a Co-C bond in coenzyme forms.

questions.question: Zinc finger proteins use a Zn2+ ion primarily to:
options: Stabilise the folded structural motif that allows the protein to bind DNA
Transport oxygen in the bloodstream
Catalyse redox reactions by cycling between Zn(I) and Zn(III)
Absorb visible light for photosynthesis
questions.correct_answer: Stabilise the folded structural motif that allows the protein to bind DNA
questions.explanation: Zinc in zinc-finger proteins is typically redox-inactive (fixed at Zn2+) and plays a structural role, coordinating cysteine/histidine residues to fold a compact motif that recognises specific DNA sequences.

questions.question: Lanthanide (4f) ions characteristically show:
options: Sharp, weak f-f electronic transitions because the 4f orbitals are shielded from the ligand environment by filled 5s and 5p orbitals
Very broad, intense d-d absorption bands typical of first-row transition metals
No characteristic optical absorption or emission at all
Bonding that is predominantly covalent and highly directional, like transition metals
questions.correct_answer: Sharp, weak f-f electronic transitions because the 4f orbitals are shielded from the ligand environment by filled 5s and 5p orbitals
questions.explanation: The 4f orbitals of lanthanides are shielded by outer 5s and 5p electrons, so they are little perturbed by the ligand field, giving sharp, Laporte-forbidden f-f transitions and largely ionic, non-directional bonding.

questions.question: The 'lanthanide contraction' refers to:
options: The steady decrease in ionic radius across the lanthanide series from La3+ to Lu3+ due to imperfect shielding by 4f electrons
The tendency of lanthanides to form smaller complexes than transition metals
A decrease in atomic number across the series
The shrinking of the lanthanide series to only seven stable elements
questions.correct_answer: The steady decrease in ionic radius across the lanthanide series from La3+ to Lu3+ due to imperfect shielding by 4f electrons
questions.explanation: As 4f electrons are added across the series they shield the increasing nuclear charge poorly, so the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons rises steadily, contracting the ionic radius from La3+ to Lu3+.

questions.question: The most common and stable oxidation state for nearly all lanthanide elements is:
questions.explanation: While some lanthanides can access +2 or +4 states (e.g. Ce4+, Eu2+), the +3 oxidation state is the characteristic and most stable state across essentially the whole lanthanide series.

questions.question: Actinide elements differ from lanthanides in that actinides:
options: Show a wider range of accessible oxidation states and greater covalent character in bonding, partly because 5f orbitals extend further and participate more in bonding
Are all non-radioactive, stable elements
Never form complexes with oxo or halide ligands
Have completely filled 5f subshells in every known ion
questions.correct_answer: Show a wider range of accessible oxidation states and greater covalent character in bonding, partly because 5f orbitals extend further and participate more in bonding
questions.explanation: Unlike the well-shielded 4f orbitals of the lanthanides, the 5f orbitals of actinides are more radially extended and can participate more in covalent bonding, giving actinides a greater variety of accessible oxidation states (e.g. uranium from +3 to +6).

questions.question: Isopoly and heteropoly acids (e.g. phosphomolybdic acid) are examples of:
options: Polyoxometalates formed by condensation of metal-oxo anions such as MoO4^2- or WO4^2-
Simple mononuclear transition-metal coordination complexes
Organometallic sandwich compounds
Lanthanide-organic frameworks
questions.correct_answer: Polyoxometalates formed by condensation of metal-oxo anions such as MoO4^2- or WO4^2-
questions.explanation: Polyoxometalates are large anionic clusters built from linked, edge- or corner-sharing MO6 octahedra of early transition metals such as Mo or W, sometimes incorporating a heteroatom such as phosphorus.

questions.question: In solid-state inorganic chemistry, a Schottky defect in an ionic crystal consists of:
options: Paired vacancies of a cation and an anion, leaving the crystal stoichiometry unchanged
An ion displaced from its normal lattice site into an interstitial site
A foreign atom substituting for a lattice ion
A dislocation line running through the crystal
questions.correct_answer: Paired vacancies of a cation and an anion, leaving the crystal stoichiometry unchanged
questions.explanation: A Schottky defect involves the loss of a stoichiometric pair of oppositely charged ions from the lattice (both moving to the surface), preserving electrical neutrality and overall stoichiometry, unlike a Frenkel defect.

questions.question: A Frenkel defect in an ionic solid arises when:
options: An ion leaves its normal lattice site and occupies an interstitial position, creating a vacancy-interstitial pair
Two cations are simultaneously removed from the lattice
A foreign ion of different charge is deliberately doped into the lattice
The crystal melts locally
questions.correct_answer: An ion leaves its normal lattice site and occupies an interstitial position, creating a vacancy-interstitial pair
questions.explanation: A Frenkel defect occurs when an ion (typically the smaller cation) migrates from its regular lattice site into an interstitial void, leaving a vacancy behind while the total number of ions is unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following ligands is classified as a 'pi-acceptor' (pi-acid) ligand because it accepts electron density from filled metal d-orbitals into its own empty pi* orbitals?
options: Carbon monoxide (CO)
Ammonia (NH3)
Fluoride (F⁻)
Water (H2O)
questions.correct_answer: Carbon monoxide (CO)
questions.explanation: CO, along with ligands like CN⁻ and phosphines, has low-lying empty π* orbitals that accept back-donated electron density from the metal, classifying it as a strong π-acceptor ligand.

questions.question: The trans effect in square planar complexes describes:
options: The ability of certain ligands to labilise (accelerate substitution of) the ligand positioned trans to them
The tendency of ligands to always occupy cis positions
A change in oxidation state of the metal upon ligand substitution
The colour change observed when a complex is heated
questions.correct_answer: The ability of certain ligands to labilise (accelerate substitution of) the ligand positioned trans to them
questions.explanation: Strong trans-directing ligands (e.g. CN⁻, CO, PR3) weaken and accelerate substitution of the ligand opposite them in square planar complexes, a kinetic effect widely exploited in synthesising Pt(II) complexes such as cisplatin.

questions.question: Cisplatin, cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2], is synthesised in preference to its trans isomer by exploiting:
options: The trans effect, starting from [PtCl4]2- and sequentially substituting to direct the correct geometry
Random mixing of Pt salts with ammonia and chloride with no mechanistic control
High-temperature solid-state fusion of the elements
Electrolysis of platinum metal in ammonia solution
questions.correct_answer: The trans effect, starting from [PtCl4]2- and sequentially substituting to direct the correct geometry
questions.explanation: The classic synthesis of cisplatin uses the trans effect: Cl⁻ is a stronger trans director than NH3, so sequential substitution starting from [PtCl4]2- can be directed to give specifically the cis isomer.

questions.question: Werner's coordination theory, foundational to inorganic complex chemistry, proposed that a metal ion exhibits:
options: Both a primary valence (oxidation state) and a secondary valence (coordination number), with the latter having a fixed spatial arrangement
Only ionic bonding with no concept of coordination number
A single type of valence identical to that of main-group elements
No fixed geometry, with ligands arranged randomly
questions.correct_answer: Both a primary valence (oxidation state) and a secondary valence (coordination number), with the latter having a fixed spatial arrangement
questions.explanation: Werner distinguished primary valence (ionisable, corresponding to oxidation state) from secondary valence (coordination number, satisfied by ligands in a fixed geometric arrangement such as octahedral), explaining the existence of isomers in coordination compounds.

questions.question: Magnetic moment measurements are useful in inorganic chemistry because they allow determination of:
options: The number of unpaired electrons in a metal complex, helping distinguish high-spin from low-spin configurations
The exact bond lengths in a complex
The colour of the complex directly
The solubility of the complex in water
questions.correct_answer: The number of unpaired electrons in a metal complex, helping distinguish high-spin from low-spin configurations
questions.explanation: The experimental magnetic moment (via the spin-only formula μ = √[n(n+2)] BM) correlates with the number of unpaired electrons n, which differs between high-spin and low-spin d-electron configurations.

questions.question: Metallocenes such as ferrocene are classified structurally as:
options: Sandwich compounds, with the metal centre held between two parallel cyclic pi-ligands
Octahedral coordination complexes with six monodentate ligands
Square planar complexes
Metal clusters with direct metal-metal bonding
questions.correct_answer: Sandwich compounds, with the metal centre held between two parallel cyclic pi-ligands
questions.explanation: Metallocenes have the characteristic 'sandwich' architecture in which a transition metal is bound between two parallel cyclopentadienyl (or related cyclic) rings via delocalised pi-bonding.

questions.question: The Wacker process, an industrially important application of organometallic catalysis, converts ethylene to:
options: Acetaldehyde, using a Pd(II)/Cu(II) catalytic system with O2 as the terminal oxidant
Ethanol, using a heterogeneous nickel catalyst
Polyethylene, using a Ziegler-Natta titanium catalyst
Vinyl chloride, using a mercury catalyst
questions.correct_answer: Acetaldehyde, using a Pd(II)/Cu(II) catalytic system with O2 as the terminal oxidant
questions.explanation: The Wacker process oxidises ethylene to acetaldehyde using a palladium(II) catalyst that is reoxidised by copper(II), with dioxygen ultimately reoxidising the copper, forming the basis of an important industrial route to acetaldehyde.

questions.question: Ziegler-Natta catalysts, widely used industrially, are best known for catalysing:
options: Stereoregular (e.g. isotactic) polymerisation of alkenes such as propene
Hydrogenation of aromatic rings only
Oxidation of alkenes to epoxides
Carbonylation of methanol to acetic acid
questions.correct_answer: Stereoregular (e.g. isotactic) polymerisation of alkenes such as propene
questions.explanation: Ziegler-Natta catalysts (typically based on titanium halides with an aluminium alkyl co-catalyst) enable controlled, stereoregular polymerisation of alkenes, producing materials such as isotactic polypropylene and high-density polyethylene.

questions.question: Superoxide dismutase (SOD), a key bioinorganic metalloenzyme, functions to:
options: Catalyse the disproportionation of the superoxide radical (O2•⁻) into O2 and H2O2, protecting cells from oxidative damage
Transport oxygen in the bloodstream
Fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia
Catalyse the hydrolysis of ATP
questions.correct_answer: Catalyse the disproportionation of the superoxide radical (O2•⁻) into O2 and H2O2, protecting cells from oxidative damage
questions.explanation: SOD enzymes (containing Cu/Zn, Mn, or Fe centres depending on the isoform) catalyse the disproportionation of the reactive superoxide radical into ordinary dioxygen and hydrogen peroxide, an essential cellular antioxidant defence.
